2. Loss Function

Your grade in this section is 3 / 3.

Consider that we are interested in finding a function f:[−10,10]→R. If we cannot write down the equation for f, we can try to approximate it by using other functions. In this class, we will use neural networks. To quantify how well a neural network can approximate the function f, we compute the distance d(f,NNP). This is known as the loss function. However, we don't know f itself, so we won't be able to compute the loss. What we know about f is some observations we have. In other words, the data D={(x1,f(x1)),…,(xN,f(xN))} is our window of observation of f. We write yi for f(xi). In this exercise, we choose D={(−2,1.8),(−1,0.2),(0,−0.3),(1,0.7),(2,1.3)}, which means we have 5 observation points. To measure how well a neural network approximates f compared to our observations, we compute the error at the observation points, loss=error at x1+⋯+error at xNN. This is called the empirical loss. The error at xi can be measured in various different ways. In this exercise, we use something called the square loss. The formula is lossD(P)=1N∑i=1N(f(xi)−NNP(xi))2.

3. Coordinate Descent

Your grade in this section is 1.75 / 2.

Training a network means finding P that makes the loss function small. Now lossD:R7→R≥0. To find the minimum of this function, we can try to find the partial derivatives and solve the system of equations ∂lossD/∂wi=0, i=1,2,…,7. But computing the derivatives here is hard with the absolute value, and solving a system of 7 equations is also pretty hard. In Section 2, we tried to minimise the loss by tweaking one parameter at a time. In this section, we do this in a more systematic way, where we start with an initial parameter, then change one parameter at a time to get the best of it, and then move to the next.

4. Training by Evolutionary Selection

Your grade in this section is 3 / 3.

In Section 3, we minimised the loss by changing one parameter at a time. When the network has many parameters, this is slow. Another approach is to change all the parameters at the same time. Now for a parameter P, we get the neural network NNP. To improve the network's performance, we change P by a bit to P+ηv, where v is the direction we move in and η>0 is the size of the step we take.

PP+ηvv: the directionη: the size of the step

If we just walk randomly, it is unlikely that we will do better. So one way is to try many directions, see which one is better, and then move along that direction. And we can repeat this process.

This is known as training by evolutionary selection, and each round is called a generation. In the following exercises, we try to approximate a function f which we observe at 30 points. In other words, we have data D with 30 samples. You can change the architecture of the network, i.e., the number of layers, the number of neurons in each layer and the activation function.

You can click between the last hidden layer and the output to add a layer. The buttons under the network allow you to choose the activation function.
